source.title: Scaling Up to Excellence: Practicing Model Scaling for Photo-Realistic Image Restoration In the Wild
source.authors: Fang-Hua Yu; Jinjin Gu; Zhe-Yuan Li; Jin-Fan Hu; Xiang-Tao Kong; Xintao Wang; Jing-Wen He; Yu Qiao; Chao Dong

record.file_problem: No apparent file problem; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses model and data scaling as a design motivation for an image-restoration system, but does not test the language-model scaling laws or fit power laws to its own results.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a qualitative training-data comparison using DIV2K, LSDIR, and the authors’ dataset (Fig. 12; §4.4). It does not report held-out cross-entropy loss, power-law fits, extrapolation from small runs, or a compute-optimal allocation sweep. Its other ablations and comparisons do not measure the claim’s specified scaling-law outcomes.
record.test_reason: SUPIR cites Kaplan et al. to motivate scaling model and data for image restoration. It reports only its own method's performance against other IR methods and ablations. There is no sweep of parameters, tokens or compute, no loss curve and no power-law fit. The training-data comparison (DIV2K vs LSDIR vs own 20M images, Fig. 12) is qualitative, figure-only, with three points and no loss measure, so it cannot bear on any version's power-law form.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors present SUPIR as an IR method empowered by model scaling, dataset enrichment and design features (ZeroSFT connector, negative-quality samples and prompts, restoration-guided sampling). They make no claim about scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains and evaluates an image-restoration system rather than measuring language-model pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.

fits_no_version.finding: Fig. 12 compares SUPIR trained on DIV2K, LSDIR and the authors' 20M-image dataset. The authors say it shows the importance of large-scale, high-quality data; there are no numbers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger, high-quality training sets qualitatively improve diffusion-prior image restoration. No functional form is established.

record.problems: The training-data comparison is qualitative and presented in a figure without numerical outcomes or uncertainty estimates. The study does not vary model size or compute to test scaling-law behavior.
record.rows_left_out: Other comparisons and ablations concern restoration methods, connectors, prompts, or sampling settings, not the scaling-law outcomes specified in the claim.

untested.parts: No held-out language-model loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small fitted runs.
No shape sweep at fixed parameter count. Trimming half of the ViT blocks in the adaptor is a design choice, not a controlled loss comparison.
Image domain, but no power-law fit and no loss measured against model or data scale.
No downstream performance as a function of scale or loss.

record.verdict_notes: Kaplan et al. is cited only as motivation ('scaling of the model requires a corresponding scaling of the training data'). Model size is never varied: SDXL at 2.6B parameters is fixed. The other quantitative results (Tables 1–2, the τr sweep, the user study) are method comparisons and are correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No prediction of larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or fitted parameter/token growth trends.
No controlled sweep of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study concerns image restoration and qualitatively compares training datasets, but does not test whether a power-law form holds in image models or other training regimes.
No study of downstream task performance as a function of pretraining loss or scale.
No comparison of scaling-law exponents, fitting choices, or curve bending.
